title: Akara Acarajé
author: Ozoz Adeniyi
desc: The Atlantic version — one cup of beans soaked no more than two to three hours, ground with onion, fried in three to four centimetres of oil.
longDesc: This is akara written as a bridge between Lagos and Bahia. The recipe is deliberately small and simple — one cup of beans, an onion, half a cup of water — and it carries one piece of advice the other version does not: soak for two to three hours and no longer, because beans left in water absorb too much of it and come out tasteless. The batter can also be rested several hours or overnight to improve its flavour, or frozen for a month. Served in Nigeria with soft white bread or ogi; in Brazil, with dried shrimp, vatapá and caruru.
ingredients: 1 cup black-eyed beans, or bean/gram flour as an alternative
1 small onion, peeled and chopped roughly
1/2 cup water, or more as needed
steps: Sort the dried beans and remove any stones and debris.
Rinse under running water, then soak 2 to 3 hours — not longer, because the beans absorb excess water and become tasteless.
Rub the beans between your hands to remove the skins. Repeat rinsing in a colander until they are nearly clean.
Grind the beans with the onions, water and chilli until a smooth thick paste forms.
Optionally rest the batter several hours or overnight to improve the flavour, or freeze it for up to a month.
Heat 3 to 4 cm of oil in a deep pan, wok or skillet.
Stir the batter and season with salt — taste to verify the salt is detectable.
Using a teaspoon, tablespoon or ice cream scoop, lower the batter gently into the hot oil. Do not overcrowd.
Fry until the underside browns, flip, and fry the other side.
chefTips: Two to three hours, no more. The reason is given: beans soaked longer absorb excess water and the akara comes out tasteless.
Taste the batter for salt before you fry. You cannot correct it afterwards and under-salted akara is flat.
Three to four centimetres of oil. Enough to float them, not enough to be a deep-fat fryer.
Resting the batter overnight genuinely improves the flavour, and it freezes for a month — useful if you want akara on a weekday morning.
European-polished beans do not give up their skins the same way West African varieties do. If the skins will not come off, bean flour or gram flour is the honest substitute.
An ice cream scoop gives the most even shape if you are not confident with a spoon.
The Brazilian version is fried in dendê — palm oil — which is the same material as Nigerian red palm oil under its Portuguese name.
commonMistakes: Soaking overnight, which washes the flavour out.
Expecting polished imported beans to peel like West African ones.
sources: Adapted from 'Akara-Acaraje: The Brazilian-Nigerian connection', Kitchen Butterfly, 9 February 2010. IMPORTANT ON ATTRIBUTION: every page fetched on that site across two independent research passes carries the byline 'Kitchen Butterfly' — the site name — and not 'Ozoz Sokoh'. Her name appears only in the footer or bio. The site is credited here accordingly, with Sokoh noted as its proprietor. Most pages on the site also report a bulk 'Modified: June 3, 2026' stamp, so modification dates there are not reliable for provenance.

Quantities as printed: 1 cup black-eyed beans (or bean/gram flour alternative), 1 small onion peeled and chopped roughly, 1/2 cup water (or more as needed), chopped chilli pepper (optional), salt to taste, optional chopped onions and dried shrimp, vegetable oil for deep frying, bread to serve.

The soaking instruction and its reason are as printed: soak 2 to 3 hours, not longer, because beans absorb excess water and become tasteless. So are the 3 to 4 cm of oil and the instruction to taste for detectable salt.
AUTHOR-DECLARED DEVIATION: she adds chopped yellow peppers for a 'hot and sweet' flavour and notes that others add dried crayfish, stock cubes and dried chilli.

ON THE ETYMOLOGY, and note that the page publishes a dissent against its own claim. The article cites Niyi Afolabi: 'through many years of enslaved Africans offering "Akara" to each other as a gesture of invitation ("Would you like to eat "Akara"?") the two words are now totally corrupted and integrated into one noun as known today: Acaraje" in Bahia today.' In the comments a reader, Femuwe, questions this as 'unlikely' semantically, and a second, Shola, argues that acarajé corresponds specifically to akara ijesha, from the western part of Nigeria, where the frying is done in palm oil as in Brazil. All three positions are recorded rather than resolved.

Nigeria against Brazil, as the page tabulates it: oil — Nigeria palm, vegetable or a mixture; Brazil dendê. Accompaniments — Nigeria soft white bread or ogi; Brazil camarão, pimenta, vatapá, caruru and salad. Acarajé received Brazilian heritage status in 2004 via IPHAN.
The bread names given on the page are 'Ojile' and 'Agebe bread', the latter almost certainly a misprint for agege (NGA036).
storage: Batter 2 days refrigerated or 1 month frozen. Fried akara, eat the same day.
reheating: Hot oven or air fryer, 5 minutes.
healthBenefits: Cowpeas supply plant protein, folate, iron and soluble fibre.
Resting the batter begins a mild fermentation that aids digestibility.
culturalNote: Akara is one of the clearest surviving threads between Yorubaland and the Black Atlantic. In Salvador the baianas de acarajé sell it from street stalls in white lace, and the dish is formally recognised Brazilian heritage; in Lagos the same fritter goes into a split of agege bread for breakfast. The argument in the comments of this very recipe — whether acarajé comes from a corrupted invitation or specifically from akara ijesha — is the kind of question food history leaves open.
